newsitem.title: UNITED NATIONS: Arab group seeks emergency U.N. assembly session.
newsitem.headline: Arab group seeks emergency U.N. assembly session.

text.p: The Arab group of states will request an emergency special session of the General Assembly on Israel's building of homes for Jews in East Jerusalem following two recent U.S. vetoes in the Security Council, the group's chairman said on Wednesday.
No date for the session has yet been set.
Speaking to reporters after a closed-door meeting of Arab envoys, Ambassador Nasser al-Khalifa of Qatar cited the General Assembly's "uniting for peace" resolution, adopted in November 1950.

This calls for holding an emergency special session of the assembly 24 hours after receipt by the secretary-general of a request supported by at least nine of the 15 Security Council members or a simple majority of the 185-member assembly.

Al-Khalifa said the group was awaiting the outcome of a meeting in Rabat, Morocco, on Thursday of the Jerusalem committee of the Organisation of the Islamic Conference, an Arab League ministerial meeting in Cairo over the weekend and a non-aligned movement meeting in New Delhi next week.

The "uniting for peace" formula was originated by the United States to enable the assembly to act "if the Security Council, because of lack of unanimity of the permanent members, fails to exercise its primary responsibility for the maintenance of international peace and security."

Washington realised the Security Council had been able to authorise troops to counter North Korea's invasion of South Korea a few months earlier only because the Soviet Union had been boycotting the council and thus deprived itself of the use of its veto. The assembly was seen then as an alternative if the council was paralysed in the future by a veto.

But more recently the shoe has been on the other foot. U.S. vetoes on March 7 and March 21 prevented action by the Security Council on a plan by Israel to build 6,500 homes for Jews on land captured during the 1967 Middle East war. The site, between Jerusalem and Bethlehem, is called Jabal Abu Ghneim in Arabic and Har Homa in Hebrew.

The assembly did adopt a resolution on March 13 by a vote of 130 to 2, with two abstentions, calling on Israel not to go ahead with the project. The United States and Israel cast the only negative votes.

Asked what would be achieved by returning to the assembly, al-Khalifa said the resulting resolution "would have more power than the last resolution. Anyhow, after the veto, where do you want us to go?"

He said the resolution was still being worked on but would "emphasize our support for peace and that we want the peace process to succeed, and that what the Israeli government is doing now is undermining the peace process."
"Unfortunately, with the veto, they seem not to listen to anybody and we want them to know that the whole world is not happy with what they are doing, and they have to listen."
